extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers using Chicago Notes & Bibliography style (academic and trade book/journal contributors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and formatting notes (footnotes/endnotes) and bibliography entries under the Chicago Notes and Bibliography system, including rules for numbering, shortened citations, placement, and special cases (editors, translators, multiauthor works, reprints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Book citation (single author) — note and bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Full note and bibliography forms for a book by a single author (examples: Cheryl Strayed, Wild...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note includes author, title, place: publisher, year, and specific page number(s). Bibliography entry inverts author name, gives full title, place: publisher, year. Follow punctuation and capitalization as shown in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with editor (ed./eds.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In notes use ed. (editor) or eds. (editors); in bibliography use 'ed.' abbreviated in note but the bibliography form does not include ed. in the shortened form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: note: Meghan Daum, ed., Selfish, Shallow, and Self-Absorbed...; bibliography: Daum, Meghan, ed. Selfish, Shallow, and Self-Absorbed.... The shortened form (subsequent citations) omits ed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with two authors — bibliography inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a book with two authors, only the first-listed name is inverted in the bibliography entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes may cite both names (Brian Grazer and Charles Fishman). Bibliography: Grazer, Brian, and Charles Fishman. Maintain word order and punctuation as for two authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with three authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliography lists all three authors with only the first name inverted; notes cite authors in normal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure shown: Berkman, Alexander, Henry Bauer, and Carl Nold. For notes, cite Berkman, Bauer, and Nold, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with four or more authors — et al. in notes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the bibliography list all authors for works with four or more authors; in notes cite only the first-listed author followed by et al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word order and punctuation in the bibliography are the same as for two or three authors; notes use 'FirstAuthor et al.' See cross-references for detailed examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with author plus editor or translator
rubrics_metrics.description: When a book has an editor or translator in addition to the author, use ed. or trans. in the note but Expanded forms (Edited by, Translated by) in the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: note: Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Love in the Time of Cholera, trans. Edith Grossman (London: Cape, 1988), 242-55. Bibliography: Garcia Marquez, Gabriel. Love in the Time of Cholera. Translated by Edith Grossman. London: Cape, 1988.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter in an edited book
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a chapter, include chapter author, chapter title in quotation marks, editor (precede book title with 'in'), and the chapter page range in the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Glenn Gould, “Streisand as Schwarzkopf,” in The Glenn Gould Reader, ed. Tim Page (New York: Vintage Books, 1984), 310. Bibliography: Gould, Glenn. “Streisand as Schwarzkopf.” In The Glenn Gould Reader, edited by Tim Page, 308–11. New York: Vintage Books, 1984.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal article citation structure (volume, issue, pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations typically include the volume and issue number and date; the volume number follows the italicized journal title in roman with no intervening punctuation; notes include specific page reference; bibliography includes the article page range preceded by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include issue number even if journal paginates consecutively across a volume; prefer DOI over general URL when available. Example: Signs 40, no. 2 (Winter 2015): 308–19. https://doi.org/...

rubrics_metrics.name: Note reference numbers: superscript in text, full size in notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Note reference numbers in text are set as superior (superscript) numbers. In the notes themselves they are normally full size, not raised, and followed by a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In manuscripts, superscript numbers in both places are acceptable (typical word-processor default). Be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols vs numbers for note references
rubrics_metrics.description: If a symbol rather than a number is used, the symbol appears as a superscript in the text but not in the note, where it is not followed by a period but may be followed by a space. Symbols become difficult as superscripts in some typefaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbols only when there are very few notes on a page or in a work. If symbols are hard to read, set them full size in the text. Sequence symbols consistently (e.g., *, †, ‡...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing of note numbers and scope of numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes, whether footnotes or endnotes, should be numbered consecutively, beginning with 1, throughout each article and for each new chapter—not throughout an entire book unless the text has no internal divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where only a handful of footnotes appear in a book, symbols may be used instead (sequence * † ‡). For scientific journals that allow repeated numbers or out-of-sequence numbers, consult Scientific Style and Format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of note number relative to punctuation and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A note number should generally be placed at the end of a sentence or at the end of a clause. It normally follows a quotation and follows any punctuation mark except for the dash, which it precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely, place the number inside closing parentheses if the note applies to a specific term within the parentheses. Example: This is what our tailors can do.²

rubrics_metrics.name: Note numbers within chapter/article titles and subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: A note number should never appear within or at the end of a chapter title. A note that applies to an entire chapter should be unnumbered and is preferably placed at the foot of the first page of the chapter, preceding any numbered notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In electronic formats that do not support footnotes, an unnumbered note might appear immediately after, or be linked from, the chapter title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple citations in one note and prohibition on multiple note references at same point
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one note reference should never appear in the same place (e.g., ³*); however, a single note can contain more than one citation or comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A note number must not reappear out of sequence; if the same substance applies to multiple locations, repeat under a new note number or use carefully checked cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use shortened citations (short form)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce bulk, subsequent citations of sources already given in full should be shortened when possible. In a work without a bibliography, repeat the full citation the first time it appears in each new chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short forms should include enough information to remind readers of the full title or to lead them to the bibliography. Cross-reference to an original full citation may help when references are far apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic structure of the short form
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common short form consists of the last name of the author and the main title of the work cited, usually shortened if more than four words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Morley, Poverty and Inequality, 43. For journal articles use author and short article title; for more on names and titles see the cited sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short form for authors' names
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the last name of the author (or of the editor or translator if given first in the full reference) is needed in the short form. Full names or initials only when needed to distinguish identical last names. For two or three authors give each last name; for more than three use first author's last name followed by et al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations such as ed. or trans. following a name in the full reference are omitted in subsequent references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short form for titles of works
rubrics_metrics.description: The short title contains the key word(s) from the main title. An initial A or The is usually omitted. The order of words should not be changed. Titles of four words or fewer are seldom shortened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short title is italicized or set in roman and quotation marks according to the full-title formatting. For foreign-language short titles retain necessary case-governing words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ibid. versus shortened citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago discourages the use of ibid. in favor of shortened citations. Ibid. traditionally refers to the work cited in the immediately preceding note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortened citations are preferred because ibid. may confuse readers in electronic formats and saves little space. With the preferred short form, a page reference must be repeated even if identical; with ibid., identical page location need not be repeated. Ibid. is capitalized at the beginning of a note and followed by a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of idem (id.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several works by the same person are cited successively in the same note, idem (sometimes abbreviated id.) has been used historically, but Chicago discourages its use outside legal references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend repeating the author’s last name instead of using idem; id. remains in place in legal citation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowance of op. cit. and loc. cit.
rubrics_metrics.description: Op. cit. and loc. cit. (used with an author’s last name to stand in for a previously cited title or place) have fallen into disuse and are disallowed by Chicago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the short-title form instead to avoid forcing readers to search back for the original full source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations plus commentary in a note
rubrics_metrics.description: When a note contains both the source of a fact or quotation and related substantive material, the source comes first. A period usually separates the citation from the commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put comments like 'emphasis mine' in parentheses. Example: Little, “Norms of Collegiality,” 330 (my italics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations within notes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a note includes a quotation, the source normally follows the terminal punctuation of the quotation. The full source need not be parenthesized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long quotations should be set off as extracts in notes as in text. In notes, more than three lines of poetry should be set off (subject to related rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive (discursive) notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive notes may amplify the text and include no sources; they may augment any system of source citation including author-date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a source is needed in a substantive note, treat it as in other note examples or parenthetically if brief and already cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing and length of notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid very long footnotes (page makeup issues); endnotes have no such bar and very long endnotes should be broken into multiple paragraphs to aid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors should consider shortening long notes or incorporating material into the text instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes that break across pages
rubrics_metrics.description: When a footnote begins on one page and continues on the next, the break should be made in midsentence; a short rule appears above the continued part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This advice applies to the published form (typesetting stage). At manuscript stage let the word processor determine breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: "See" vs "cf." usage in notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'see' to invite consultation of further resources; use 'cf.' only to mean 'compare' or 'see, by way of comparison.' Neither term is italicized in notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For further discussion, see Jones, Conflict, 49. Others disagree; cf. Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes, 101–3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes versus endnotes — pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes: preferred by readers for ease of reference and where notes are closely integrated into the text. Endnotes: avoid page makeup issues and can make pages less intimidating to general readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may recommend endnotes for marketing reasons; authors should balance text and notes and avoid excessive discursive notes. Endnotes make locating a particular note harder unless mitigated by running heads or links in electronic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endnote placement and grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Endnotes to each chapter are often best grouped in the end matter, following text and appendixes and preceding the bibliography. The main heading is 'Notes' and each chapter’s notes are introduced by a subhead with chapter number or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multiauthor books or chapters offered separately, place endnotes at the end of each chapter. In journals, endnotes appear at the end of each article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running heads for endnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where endnotes gather at the back and occupy more than a few pages, running heads showing the page numbers to which the notes pertain are helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine numbers for a running head, find the first and last notes beginning on that page, locate their references in the main text, and use the numbers of the first and last text pages on which those references appear (e.g., 'Notes to Pages 123–125'). Last number not abbreviated. Running heads can be completed only at page-proof stage and may be charged as alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for endnotes (repeat key info)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because endnotes are separated from text, omit less at the risk of irritating readers; repeat the author (or at least last name) and title in endnotes unless clear from text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing ibid. in endnotes where readers must flip back. Consolidate some endnote references or include helpful running heads. If a source is clearly identified in the text, a parenthetical reference in the endnote may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two sets of notes (substantive vs citation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In heavily documented works, it may be helpful to separate substantive notes from source citations: citation notes numbered and appearing as endnotes; substantive notes indicated by symbols and appearing as footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First footnote on each printed page referenced by an asterisk. Sequence symbols if multiple on a page (e.g., *, †, ‡; then **, †† for 4th–6th). Adaptations may be needed in electronic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes plus author-date citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of symbols, use author-date citations in text for sources and numbered footnotes/endnotes for substantive comments; numbered notes can themselves contain parenthetical author-date citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach reduces complexity and adds flexibility; see chapter on author-date for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor's or translator's added notes vs original author's notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes added by an editor or translator must be distinguished from the author's original notes. Commonly the added notes are interspersed and consecutively numbered with the original notes but distinguished by appending '—Ed.' or '—Trans.' or by enclosing the added note in square brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, added notes can be referenced by asterisks and appear as footnotes preceding the author's numbered notes. When only a few added notes exist, symbols can be used for the additions and the original notes numbered normally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnumbered notes (epigraphs, chapter-wide notes, source notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnumbered footnotes always precede any numbered notes on the same page and most often appear on the opening page of a chapter (e.g., epigraph source). In works with endnotes, an unnumbered endnote can appear immediately before note 1 if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unnumbered notes for chapter-wide source notes, biographical notes, acknowledgments, or epigraph citations. In electronic formats unnumbered notes might be linked from the element to which they pertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes keyed to text by line or page numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In some works (e.g., editions of classics or verse) omit note numbers in the text and key notes to the text by line or page numbers (sometimes followed by the word or phrase being annotated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line numbers are used only if they appear in the text. Such keyed notes are a publisher’s nicety and more easily implemented in print; in electronic formats links are preferable. With prose, notes cannot be numbered until typeset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source notes for previously published material (reprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: In anthologies or collections of previously published material, give the source of each reprinted piece in an unnumbered footnote on the first printed page of the chapter, preceding numbered notes. For material still in copyright, include original title, publisher/journal, date, page numbers or locators, and mention of permission to reprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a copyright notice if requested by the permissions grantor; some grantors demand particular language. Wording can be adjusted for consistency as long as proper credit is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: If an article/chapter is reprinted under a different title or revised
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide original publication details and indicate 'Reprinted by permission' or 'Originally published in a slightly different form in...' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Originally published as "Manet in His Generation...," Critical Inquiry 19, no. 1 (1992): 22–69. © 1992 by The University of Chicago. Reprinted by permission.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical notes and acknowledgments placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief biographical notes on authors often appear as unnumbered notes on the first page of each article/chapter or at the end of the chapter; acknowledgments can be given similarly in an unnumbered note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such identifying notes are unnecessary when a list of contributors with affiliations is provided. Keep biographical notes brief.
